claims.words: I believe humans will become cyborgs and no longer be stand-alone entities.
claims.claimed: The 1998 implant, he says, was a test of whether information could pass to and from an implant; it did, and for nine days doors opened and lights came on as he walked through his department. From that he argues that highly intelligent machines will overtake people later this century, that linking people to those machines by implant is a natural next step that would make superhumans in effect, and that the alternative is machines ruling and people as second-class citizens. He also predicts thought-to-thought communication replacing speech. Hedged as belief and envisioning throughout; the plan for a second implant linked to his wife and an internet link from New York are stated as intentions, not results. The essay opens with the line, often quoted, that he was born human by accident of fate; that line is really there, as its first words.

claims.claimed: Three routes are weighed. Whole brain emulation (pages 30 to 34): scanning, translation and simulation; he says there is good reason to think the enabling technologies are attainable though not soon, and that a first emulation would likely be imperfect; no date is attached. Biological enhancement (pages 38 to 43 and 50): iterated embryo selection is set out step by step, could select strongly for several traits at once, and seems to him an especially promising technology, though slow and gradual next to machine intelligence; cohorts enhanced this way could be adults by mid-century (page 43). Brain-computer interfaces (pages 44 to 51): implants could let people borrow the strengths of digital computing, but he thinks it unlikely they will be widely used as enhancements any time soon, and argues (page 46) that the limiting step in human intelligence is not how fast data can be fed into the brain but how quickly the brain can make sense of it, so more input bandwidth would do little unless the brain's own machinery were upgraded. He allows the cyborg route is not without promise, citing a rat hippocampus prosthesis (page 47).

claims.claimed: His own claim is that the merge has already started and is a few years in, that it will be gradual, and that it will probably come sooner than most people think; he gives no year of his own. The 2025 to 2075 range in the post is explicitly other people's guesses, not his. The forms he names: phones, feeds and search already steering us; co-evolution in which AI designs the chips that improve AI; and superhuman AI, genetic enhancement and brain-machine interfaces, which he says are going to happen. His line of alternatives is electrodes in the brain or becoming very close friends with a chatbot. Hedges and conditions: it probably cannot be stopped, unless we destroy ourselves first; the merge is probably the best case against the alternative of two species competing for dominance; his guess is that we are either the biological bootloader for digital intelligence or we work out a successful merge; and he calls for worldwide coordination.

claims.words: knowingly trading away one or more of your essential properties would be tantamount to suicide
claims.claimed: Framing hedge first: the piece is published under the newspaper's label of fiction, set in an imagined Manhattan clinic selling an enhancement bundle it calls Merge, so its claims are offered as an imagined future rather than a forecast; the argument itself is hers. Two possible ceilings on merging with AI. A consciousness ceiling: if microchips turn out to be the wrong material for consciousness (which she assumes for the sake of argument), replacing brain parts with chips would diminish or end your life as a conscious being, and because working memory and attention seem tied to consciousness, we may be stuck with our existing bandwidth limits. A self ceiling: the mind-is-software view does not hold, since programs are abstract objects while minds act in space and time, so there is no ground for confidence that the self survives a merge or even less radical enhancements. She hedges explicitly that we do not know whether there is a self ceiling or where it sits, and closes by asking for humility. She does not say partial enhancement is safe; she says it is uncertain.

claims.words: we predict that Musk's brain will communicate with the computer at about 10 bits/s
claims.claimed: The paper estimates that human behaviour carries information at about 10 bits a second across the tasks it examines (typing, speaking, memory contests and others), while the senses gather about a billion, and it says the gap is unexplained. In the section on Musk it calls the feeling that our inner life is much richer than we can express "the Musk illusion", quotes Musk saying Neuralink's purpose is a high-bandwidth interface "such that we can be symbiotic with AI" because "we have a bandwidth problem", and predicts that Musk's brain, linked to a computer, would communicate at about 10 bits a second; a telephone, it says, would do as well. The next section, on brain-computer interfaces for patients, says such devices "could greatly benefit" people who struggle to speak, and that "one really needs to convey only a few bits per second to and from the brain". Hedges: the authors call the cause of the limit an open question and propose research to explain it; the prediction about Musk rests on the research they review, not on a measurement of an implant.

claims.notes: Replies searched for on 2026-10-23 (letters in Neuron, preprints, commentary by brain-computer interface researchers): no formal published reply was found. Two pushbacks were. Britton Sauerbrei, a neuroscientist at Case Western Reserve University, told The New York Times (2024-12-26) that the estimate leaves out the unconscious signals the body uses to stand, walk or recover from a trip, which would give "a vastly higher bit rate", while finding the argument "pretty airtight" for conscious tasks. Matt Angle, on the blog of the implant company Paradromics (2025-09-19, https://paradromics.com/blog/the-speed-of-human-thought-and-its-implications-for-brain-computer-interfaces/, read on 2026-10-23), accepts the low rate but argues that reading it out of the brain still takes detailed recordings, and that restoring sight, or a more natural feel of controlling a robotic limb, needs more than a few bits a second; the company makes high-bandwidth implants.

Third-party pages from 2024 quote an earlier version of the mission that spoke of a generalized brain interface restoring autonomy today and unlocking human potential tomorrow; that older wording was not retrieved from the company's own site and is listed as secondary.
claims.bears_on_note: The log's introduction places the Musk and Neuralink entries on the link-to-machines branch; the entry itself names no leaf.
claims.why_here: It is the company's current public statement of purpose, and the gap between it and the 2019 to 2020 statements (reducing the existential threat of AI as the point of the company) is itself part of the record.
